endorsements.quote: Trainees remain responsible for reviewing primary sources and assessing their validity and applicability.
Require human validation of any natural language processing used for thematic analysis of feedback.
Preserve human oversight for all consequential recruitment decisions, limiting AI applications to initial triage and administrative tasks.

Require psychiatry-specific validation (i.e., comparison with human reviewers) of AI-assisted screening before implementation, recognizing that confirmatory review of screen-in applications is insufficient (remains unknown who is incorrectly screened out) and that our specialty’s emphasis on narrative assessment and interpersonal competencies differs substantially from other medical disciplines [21, 22].
Implement continuous bias auditing and outcome monitoring to identify and mitigate algorithmic perpetuation of systemic inequities.
Adding an inter disciplinary AI Council to govern policy and ethics, and embed it with early AI adopters who provide hands-on, discipline-specific support at the program level.

(a) Institutional governance structures (e.g., Chief AI Officer) must include explicit conflict of interest disclosure and independence from vendor relationships, given faculty development decisions shape downstream tool adoption across the institution;
Faculty AI literacy cur ricula must include not only operational skill-building Academic Psychiatry but also explicit instruction on AI limitations;

Providing educational content to facilitate AI literacy among faculty, including its dissemination through Learning Management System (LMS) platforms to enable asynchronous, self-paced engagement across career stages and clinical schedules.

Adopt an incremental access model for AI documentation tools, progressing from restricted use during PGY1–2 when documentation skills are still being acquired to Academic Psychiatry graduated access as trainees demonstrate competency in accurate clinical documentation and case formulation, thereby preventing un-skilling or mis-skilling while optimizing efficiency.

Given that documentation itself is a critical element in training [27], residency programs must differentiate between cognitive offloading that aids efficiency and deskilling that undermines acquisition of clinical reasoning skills.
Train trainees to obtain informed consent for AI tools and use only HIPAA-compliant protocols in clinical settings, with particular attention to patient privacy and trust.

Disseminate (or create, if not available) clear institutional guidelines delineating appropriate vs. Inappropriate AI use in educational contexts, with particular attention to maintaining academic integrity in curriculum design and assessment.

(a) processing of applicant data on private, secure serv ers with institutional review of vendor data-handling, model training, and retention policies, applicant privacy and FERPA-relevant protections remain essential;

(a) the small size of many psychiatry residency programs creates a meaningful de-identification risk, requiring de-identification protocols and institutional review of data-handling practices that preserve anonymity,
(c) Protected time and access to AI tools must be distributed equitably across faculty ranks, tracks, and demographic groups, to prevent AI fluency from becoming a new axis of academic inequity;

When available recruitment tools do not yet meet these conditions, the appropriate response is to defer adoption, advocate for these standards, and pilot tools in limited, lower-stakes contexts (e.g., administrative triage) rather than proceed with full implementation.

Creating dedicated AI education research funding mechanisms, while simultaneously embedding AI-related aims into existing grant portfolios across clinical, educational, and health services research to normalize and promote AI scholarship.

unlisted_practices: Maintain transparency with applicants about AI use in screening, including disclosure of data collection, storage, and third-party access.
Disclose to trainees when and how AI tools contribute to their evaluations, including algorithmic inputs and the relative weight of AI versus faculty assessments.
Obtain explicit informed consent from trainees for AI use of their data, with opt-out provisions that do not penalize declining.
Reserve high-stakes trainee assessments for faculty review and limit AI to structured, lower-stakes assessments.
Do not use trainee data in AI-assisted program evaluation until anonymization protocols and opt-in consent frameworks are established.
Introduce AI tools to trainees in a staged manner aligned with their developmental level, preserving bedside teaching, supervision, and face-to-face feedback.
Conduct longitudinal assessments comparing trainee outcomes between AI-supplemented and traditional curricula.
Establish baseline metrics to assess whether AI tools improve educational outcomes, efficiency, or both.
Treat AI-generated inferences about program culture as hypotheses requiring human input.
Protect faculty time so they can engage in AI training and literacy courses.
Obtain informed consent from patients for AI tools used in clinical learning settings.
Use AI to enhance rather than replace educator-learner and patient-clinician relationships.

screen.reason: An editorial/framework commentary offering recommendations and governance strategies for integrating AI into psychiatry graduate medical education.
